passage: I'm Gurleen, Kishore's cousin, and we grew up in the same building in Ludhiana. This year he applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan. "Why waste fees on backups?" he said. "They'll take me." When his mother suggested two more colleges, he laughed. He even told his manager he'd be leaving in August and sold his old bike to a neighbour. I didn't say much. He sounded so sure, and I don't really know how admissions work. The email came on a Tuesday. Rejected. He didn't come down for dinner for two days. When I finally knocked, he said, "I never even thought about this happening." I don't know what he's planning now.

qa.q: How many master's programmes did Kishore apply to?
qa.a: Kishore applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan.

qa.q: Why does the rejection hurt Kishore so much?
qa.a: He never allowed any doubt and had already told his manager and sold his bike, so the rejection lands with no plan and nothing to cushion it.

qa.q: What could Kishore do differently when planning the next round?
qa.a: He could keep his hopes but add a margin: apply to a few programmes, keep his job until an offer comes, and ask what he'd do if the first choice says no.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel watching this happen?
qa.a: Gurleen seems sad and a little guilty for staying quiet, and unsure how to help now that Kishore is shaken. 🤍

grounding: Shows a young man so sure of one admission that he left no margin, so the rejection hurts far more.

passage:
Two weeks before: Manoj put all his savings, twelve thousand rupees, into ingredients for a momo stall at the college fest. "We'll sell out by noon," he told Siddharth. "No need to keep anything aside." When Siddharth asked about rain, Manoj waved it away.
Fest day: It poured from eleven. Half the crowd went home. The stall sold forty plates out of three hundred, and there was no freezer for the rest.
Three days later: Manoj sat on the hostel steps holding the stall's unpaid electricity bill. "If I'd even once imagined it going wrong," he said, "I'd have kept some money back. I never let myself think it."

qa.q: How many plates did the stall sell?
qa.a: The stall sold forty plates out of three hundred.

qa.q: What does Manoj's line "I never let myself think it" reveal?
qa.a: It shows he now sees that his certainty kept him from imagining failure, and that the missing doubt is part of why the loss hurts so much.

qa.q: What could Manoj do before his next plan?
qa.a: He could list what might go wrong, like rain, and keep some money aside or buy stock in smaller batches, so one bad day costs less.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth after his question about rain was waved away?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel sorry for Manoj and a bit frustrated, since the risk he raised is exactly what happened.

grounding: Shows a young adult so certain a plan will work that he leaves no margin, and how much harder the failure hits.

passage: Harsha, you say you're completely sure about this job and the flat and everything. Let your Uday mama tell you about twenty-one-year-old me. I was certain Leena and I would marry. I had planned it all: the city, the job near her college, even names for children. When my father asked what I'd do if things changed, I got angry and left the room. I turned down a good posting in Pune because it was far from her. Then in my final year she told me she wanted a different life. It was nobody's fault. But because I had never let a single doubt in, I had nothing to lean on. It took me two years to stand straight again.

qa.q: Which posting did Uday turn down?
qa.a: Uday turned down a good posting in Pune because it was far from Leena.

qa.q: Why did young Uday get angry when his father asked what he'd do if things changed?
qa.a: He was so sure of the future that even a question about doubt felt like an attack on it, so he pushed it away instead of thinking about it.

qa.q: What could Harsha take from Uday mama's story about the new job and flat?
qa.a: Harsha can stay hopeful but ask what would happen if the plan changed, and keep some options open, so a surprise doesn't knock everything down.

qa.q: How might Uday's father have felt when his son left the room?
qa.a: His father probably felt worried and helpless, seeing his son build everything on one certainty and refuse any question about it.

grounding: Shows a young man so sure a relationship would last that he left no margin, so the loss hurt far more.

passage: The hostel allotment list went up at six on a stormy evening, and Usha's name wasn't on it. She read it twice, rain dripping off the notice board's plastic cover. She had been so sure. "I'm in the top twenty of the batch, they always take the top twenty," she'd told everyone. So she had given notice on her rented room, which ended tomorrow. She hadn't looked at any other rooms. When Imran had asked, "What if the list is different this year?" she had laughed. Now her two bags were packed, the auto drivers weren't coming out in this rain, and she had nowhere to sleep tomorrow night. Imran found her under the canteen awning, staring at nothing. "I didn't even let myself think it could go wrong," she said. "That's why it feels like the floor fell." He handed her his umbrella. "Let's call your old landlord first."

qa.q: What time did the hostel allotment list go up?
qa.a: At six on a stormy evening.

qa.q: Why does Usha say it feels like "the floor fell"?
qa.a: She had been completely certain and never allowed any doubt, so she made no backup plan. The shock is bigger because she had no room in her mind for this outcome.

qa.q: What choice earlier could have left Usha some margin, and what should she do first now?
qa.a: Earlier, she could have kept looking at other rooms or waited to give notice until the list came out. Now, calling the old landlord first, as Imran suggests, is a sensible step.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when he finds Usha under the canteen awning?
qa.a: He is probably sorry for her and a little worried, and chooses practical help over saying "I told you so."

grounding: A student so sure of a hostel seat gives up her room with no backup, and the rejection hurts more because she never allowed doubt.

passage: Kavitha had already bought the frame for the certificate. The college's startup grant would be announced on Friday, and she was certain her project, a repair-and-resell shop for old school uniforms in Chennai, would win. She'd told her parents at dinner. She'd borrowed three thousand from her cousin to print banners with "Winner" left blank to fill in later. When her friend Ayesha said, "Maybe keep a plan B, just in case?" Kavitha said, "Why plan to lose?" On Friday, in the packed seminar hall, the names were read out. Hers wasn't one of them. She sat through the claps with a fixed smile. Outside by the bike stand she finally cried. "It's not just losing," she told Ayesha. "I made everyone believe it too. And I have no idea what to do on Monday." Ayesha put an arm around her shoulders and waited.

qa.q: What had Kavitha already bought before the announcement?
qa.a: The frame for the certificate.

qa.q: Why is losing so painful for Kavitha?
qa.a: She had been so sure that she told her parents, borrowed money and printed banners, leaving no space for doubt. Now she faces the loss plus the embarrassment of having no plan.

qa.q: When Ayesha suggested a plan B, what choice could Kavitha have made instead?
qa.a: She could have said, "Good idea," and quickly listed what she would do if she didn't win, such as other grants or starting smaller, without giving up hope.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel standing with Kavitha by the bike stand?
qa.a: Ayesha probably feels sad for Kavitha and chooses to comfort her quietly instead of reminding her of the plan B conversation.

grounding: A student certain she will win a startup grant makes no backup plan and is hurt more deeply when she loses.
